History and Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
65-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes awoke ~1 hour prior to call with painless complete inability to move his left arm, left facial tingling, mild dysarthria and dysphagia; GP strongly suspects acute stroke and has arranged immediate ambulance transfer to hospital stroke team.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Sudden painless inability to move left arm noted on awakening today (≈1 hr before consultation).  
• Course: Persistent; no improvement; speech difficulty reported to be worsening during call.  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Tingling/paresthesia of left facial side since onset.  
  – Mild dysphagia (spilled drink).  
  – Mild dysarthria (slowed, effortful speech).  
  – No left-leg weakness, no facial droop appreciated by patient, no headache, no loss of consciousness, no discoloration or coolness of limb.  
• Exacerbating/relieving factors: None identified; denies awkward sleeping position.  
• Review of systems (pertinent negatives/positives as above); other systems not discussed.

Past Medical History:
• Type 2 diabetes mellitus.  
• Hypertension.

Medications:  
• Metformin – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Losartan – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Amlodipine – dose/route/frequency not documented.

Allergies:
• Penicillin (reaction details not documented).

Social History:
• Lives alone.  
• Former smoker (quantity/quit date not documented).  
• Alcohol: “A few pints on weekends and a couple during the week” (beer).  
• No other substance use mentioned.

Family History:
• Father: “heart disease” (details unknown).  
• No other familial conditions reported.

Physical Examination:
• Conducted via telephone; no direct examination or vitals available.  
• Patient reports no visible facial asymmetry.

Investigations:
• None performed prior to transfer.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Suspected Acute Cerebrovascular Event (likely ischemic stroke; hemorrhage less likely but cannot be excluded):  
• Sudden focal neurological deficits (left arm paralysis, left facial paresthesia, dysarthria, dysphagia) with vascular risk factors.  
Plan:  
  – Emergency medical services arranged; ambulance en route.  
  – Patient instructed to unlock door and wait seated in hallway; clinician remained on line until EMS arrival.  
  – Anticipated hospital management: urgent brain imaging (non-contrast CT ± CTA), stroke team evaluation for IV thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy as appropriate (per transcript: “they will ring through for the stroke doctor to assess… to see whether they can give you any kind of treatment”).  

Issue 2 – Chronic Hypertension and Type 2 Diabetes (stroke risk factors):  
• No acute management changes discussed during call.  
Plan:  
  – Long-term optimization to be addressed after acute event; not priority during emergency.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute ischemic stroke – High likelihood: classic abrupt unilateral deficits with speech/swallowing involvement in patient with HTN/DM; symptoms persistent and possibly worsening.  
2. Intracerebral hemorrhage – Moderate likelihood: identical sudden presentation; HTN is a risk factor, but absence of headache or altered consciousness makes less likely.  
3. Transient ischemic attack – Moderate but decreasing likelihood: same initial presentation but deficits >1 hr and worsening, making completed stroke more probable.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing expected elements: objective vitals, physical exam, last-known-well time clarification, blood glucose, medication doses/routes/frequencies, allergy reaction details.  
• Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
• Transcript quality: Clear; minor conversational overlaps but medically complete for emergency context.
